q: The formula (x1 ∨ ¬x2 ∨ x3) ∧ (¬x1 ∨ x2 ∨ x3) ∧ (x1 ∨ x2 ∨ ¬x3) is converted to a clique instance: one vertex per literal occurrence, and an edge between two vertices exactly when they are in different clauses and are not complementary literals. How many edges does the graph have?
explain:
There are 3 clauses with 3 literals each, so 3 × (3 · 3) = 27 pairs of vertices in different clauses. Remove the complementary pairs:

C1 x1  – C2 ¬x1      C1 ¬x2 – C2 x2
C1 ¬x2 – C3 x2       C1 x3  – C3 ¬x3
C2 x3  – C3 ¬x3      C2 ¬x1 – C3 x1

27 − 6 = 21.

q: A graph G has 10 vertices, and its largest clique has 4 vertices. What is the size of a minimum vertex cover of the complement graph of G?
explain: S is a clique in G if and only if V − S is a vertex cover of the complement. So the minimum cover has size n − (maximum clique) = 10 − 4 = 6.

q: Let A ≤ₚ B denote a polynomial-time reduction from A to B. Suppose A is NP-complete and B is in NP. Which statement is correct?
explain: Every NP problem reduces to A, and A reduces to B. Reductions compose, so B is NP-hard. Together with B ∈ NP, B is NP-complete.

q: Assume P ≠ NP. Which of the following statements are true?
options: 3-SAT cannot be solved in polynomial time
2-SAT can be solved in polynomial time
Every problem in NP is NP-complete
explain: (A) If 3-SAT were in P, every NP problem would be, so P = NP. (B) 2-SAT is in P whatever the answer to P vs NP. (C) is false: problems in P are in NP but not NP-complete when P ≠ NP. (D) is true: any NP problem can be reduced to halting.
